title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Fluids, Insulin, Potassium
bottomLine: DKA is a dehydration, acidosis, and electrolyte emergency. Treatment centers on IV fluids, insulin, and careful potassium monitoring; falling glucose alone does not mean the ketoacidosis is resolved.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity breath, and Kussmaul respirations are classic clues.
Potassium may be normal or high initially despite total-body potassium depletion.
Infection and missed insulin are common triggers.
priorities: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, hydration, and cardiac rhythm.
Begin ordered isotonic fluids and insulin protocol.
Monitor potassium closely and replace only according to the treatment protocol.
assessMonitor: Trend glucose, electrolytes, bicarbonate/anion gap, renal function, intake/output, vital signs, and neurologic status.
Monitor cardiac rhythm when potassium is significantly abnormal.
interventions: Add dextrose to fluids when ordered as glucose falls so insulin can continue until ketosis/acidosis resolves.
Treat the precipitating cause.
medicationSafety: Insulin can rapidly lower potassium.
Do not start or continue IV insulin in severe hypokalemia until potassium is addressed per protocol.
teaching: Reinforce sick-day rules, ketone testing when directed, hydration, never stopping basal insulin without instruction, and early help for persistent vomiting or high ketones.
delegationScope: Frequent glucose checks may be delegated where policy permits, but DKA is unstable and requires licensed-nurse assessment and close RN/provider collaboration.
examTrap: Stopping insulin as soon as glucose reaches the target while acidosis and ketones persist.
oneLinePearl: In DKA, close the gap—not just the glucose.
sourceBasis: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care in Diabetes

title: Thyroid Storm: Hypermetabolic Emergency
bottomLine: Thyroid storm is severe thyrotoxicosis with systemic decompensation. High fever, marked tachycardia, agitation/delirium, GI symptoms, heart failure, or shock in a hyperthyroid patient requires emergency escalation.
recognize: Very high fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation, delirium, vomiting/diarrhea, and heart failure are high-yield clues.
Triggers include infection, surgery, trauma, and abrupt discontinuation of antithyroid therapy.
priorities: Activate emergency response and assess ABCs, temperature, rhythm, perfusion, and mental status.
Begin cooling/supportive measures and prescribed medications rapidly.
assessMonitor: Continuous rhythm and hemodynamic monitoring in acute care.
Trend temperature, fluid status, glucose, and neurologic status.
interventions: Use cooling measures and IV fluids as ordered.
Prepare/administer beta blockade, antithyroid medication, iodine after thionamide, and glucocorticoid per protocol.
medicationSafety: Iodine is given after antithyroid medication in thyroid storm protocols.
Beta blockers may be unsafe in shock or severe decompensated heart failure and require clinician-directed use.
teaching: After stabilization, reinforce medication adherence and prompt treatment of infection or severe hyperthyroid symptoms.
delegationScope: This is an emergency; the PN initiates supportive actions within policy and immediately escalates to RN/provider/rapid response.
examTrap: Treating the fever as a routine infection symptom without recognizing the hypermetabolic syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Hyperthyroid plus fever, delirium, and racing heart: think storm.

title: Acute Kidney Injury: Trend Output, Potassium, and Volume
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: AKI may first appear as reduced urine output or rising creatinine, but the immediate nursing threats are hyperkalemia, fluid overload, uremic complications, and worsening perfusion. Trend the patient, not one lab value.
recognize: Oliguria, edema, rising creatinine, nausea, confusion, or new hypertension may occur.
AKI can be prerenal from hypoperfusion, intrinsic renal, or postrenal from obstruction.
priorities: Assess perfusion, volume status, urine output, medications, and signs of obstruction.
Report rapidly falling urine output, hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, or neurologic change promptly.
Avoid nephrotoxic exposures when possible and ordered.
assessMonitor: Strict intake/output, daily weight, blood pressure, edema, lung sounds, potassium, creatinine, and acid-base status as ordered.
interventions: Implement the ordered fluid strategy based on cause and volume status.
Follow renal-dose medication adjustments and avoid unnecessary potassium/phosphate loads.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen renal perfusion in vulnerable patients.
Renally cleared drugs may accumulate and require dose adjustment.
teaching: Teach avoidance of unapproved NSAIDs and nephrotoxic supplements, hydration guidance specific to the plan, and follow-up labs.
delegationScope: Routine urine measurement and weights may be delegated with exact reporting thresholds.
Interpretation of abrupt output changes requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Automatically giving more fluid to every oliguric patient without checking for fluid overload or obstruction.
oneLinePearl: AKI: watch potassium, lungs, and urine output together.

title: Hemodialysis Access: Protect the Lifeline
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: An AV fistula or graft is the patient's dialysis lifeline. Assess for patency and infection, and avoid blood pressure measurements, venipuncture, IV access, constriction, and unnecessary pressure on that extremity.
recognize: A functioning access usually has a palpable thrill and audible bruit.
Loss of thrill/bruit, severe bleeding, erythema, drainage, swelling, or cool distal extremity are abnormal.
priorities: Check thrill/bruit as ordered and inspect the site.
Protect the access arm from compression and invasive procedures.
Escalate absent thrill/bruit or uncontrolled bleeding immediately.
assessMonitor: Assess access patency, distal circulation, signs of infection, and post-dialysis bleeding.
Monitor pre/post-dialysis weight and blood pressure as ordered.
interventions: Apply gentle direct pressure to post-dialysis bleeding per protocol without occluding flow.
Maintain infection-control technique around dialysis access.
medicationSafety: Antihypertensive timing may be adjusted around dialysis to reduce intradialytic hypotension; follow orders.
Many medications require renal dosing or dialysis timing.
teaching: Teach the patient to check the access daily, avoid sleeping on the arm or tight clothing, and report loss of thrill or prolonged bleeding.
delegationScope: Protective precautions can be reinforced by all staff, but access assessment is a licensed-nurse responsibility within scope.
examTrap: Taking a blood pressure on the fistula arm because the other arm has an IV.
oneLinePearl: No BP, sticks, or pressure on the dialysis access arm.
sourceBasis: National Kidney Foundation Hemodialysis Access Guidance

title: Acute Stroke: Time, Airway, and Last Known Well
bottomLine: Sudden focal neurologic deficit is a stroke emergency. Determine the exact last-known-well time, protect airway and swallowing, check glucose, and activate the stroke pathway immediately.
recognize: Face droop, arm weakness, speech change, visual loss, neglect, ataxia, or sudden severe neurologic deficit may indicate stroke.
Hypoglycemia can mimic stroke and must be checked rapidly.
Posterior circulation stroke may present with severe dizziness, ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, or vomiting.
priorities: Activate stroke response/EMS immediately.
Determine last known well and symptom onset details.
Check glucose and assess airway, breathing, circulation, and neurologic status.
Keep NPO until swallow safety is established.
assessMonitor: Frequent neurologic and vital-sign monitoring in acute care.
Watch for worsening headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, aspiration, or new deficits.
interventions: Maintain head/neck alignment and aspiration precautions.
Prepare for urgent brain imaging and reperfusion evaluation.
medicationSafety: Do not give food, oral medications, or fluids until swallow safety is known.
Antithrombotic and blood-pressure management depend on stroke type and reperfusion plan and require acute-care orders.
teaching: Reinforce FAST/BE-FAST recognition, medication adherence, smoking cessation, and rehabilitation participation after stabilization.
delegationScope: Do not delegate evaluation of new focal neurologic symptoms.
The PN recognizes the change, initiates emergency actions, and immediately escalates.
examTrap: Giving water to test swallowing before the formal swallow screen is completed.
oneLinePearl: Stroke: last known well, glucose, NPO, activate now.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association/American Stroke Association Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidance

title: Seizure Safety and Postictal Care
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: During a seizure, protect the patient from injury, maintain airway safety, time the event, and never restrain or place objects in the mouth. A prolonged seizure or repeated seizures without recovery is status epilepticus and needs emergency treatment.
recognize: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures cause loss of consciousness, stiffening, rhythmic jerking, and a postictal period.
Focal seizures may cause staring, automatisms, sensory symptoms, or localized motor activity.
priorities: Lower to a safe surface if needed and protect the head.
Turn to the side when possible and clear nearby hazards.
Time the seizure and observe features.
Afterward assess airway, breathing, oxygenation, glucose when indicated, injury, and neurologic recovery.
assessMonitor: Document duration, movements, eye/head deviation, continence, triggers, medications, and postictal state.
Monitor for recurrence and respiratory depression after rescue medication.
interventions: Loosen restrictive clothing and provide oxygen/suction as needed after convulsive activity when safe.
Administer rescue benzodiazepine per order/protocol for prolonged seizure.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can depress respirations and blood pressure.
Antiseizure medications should not be stopped abruptly unless specifically directed.
redFlags: Seizure lasting about 5 minutes or longer
teaching: Teach medication adherence, seizure first aid, trigger/sleep management, and safety restrictions per clinician/state guidance.
delegationScope: Any staff member can call for help and protect the patient from injury, but licensed-nurse assessment and rescue-medication administration follow scope and policy.
examTrap: Putting a tongue blade or padded object between the teeth.
oneLinePearl: Protect, side, time—nothing in the mouth.
sourceBasis: American Epilepsy Society Status Epilepticus Guidance

title: Increased Intracranial Pressure: Protect Perfusion
bottomLine: A declining level of consciousness is an early and important sign of worsening intracranial pressure. Prevent secondary injury by maintaining oxygenation, neutral head alignment, appropriate head elevation, and rapid escalation of neurologic decline.
recognize: Early signs include headache, vomiting, behavior change, restlessness, and declining consciousness.
Late Cushing response may include widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, and abnormal respirations.
priorities: Assess airway, breathing, neurologic status, pupils, and vital signs.
Elevate head of bed as ordered, keep head midline, and avoid neck/hip flexion that impairs venous drainage.
Escalate any acute neurologic decline immediately.
assessMonitor: Frequent GCS/LOC, pupils, motor response, vital signs, oxygenation, and seizure activity.
interventions: Minimize unnecessary stimulation and cluster care when appropriate.
Avoid routine suctioning unless clinically necessary because coughing can transiently raise ICP.
medicationSafety: Hyperosmolar therapy requires close fluid, electrolyte, renal, and hemodynamic monitoring.
Sedatives can obscure neurologic examination and require ordered monitoring.
teaching: After stabilization, teach the reason for activity, positioning, and stimulation restrictions.
delegationScope: Routine comfort care may be delegated when stable, but neurologic assessments and response to acute change require licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Placing the patient flat with hips flexed to improve comfort despite worsening neurologic status.
oneLinePearl: ICP rises when venous drainage is blocked—head up, head midline.
sourceBasis: Neurocritical Care Society Cerebral Edema Guidance

title: GI Bleeding: Perfusion Before the Stool Color
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In GI bleeding, hemodynamic status matters more than whether blood is bright red or black. Tachycardia, orthostasis, hypotension, syncope, falling hemoglobin, or altered mentation signal significant blood loss and require rapid escalation.
recognize: Hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis suggests upper GI bleeding; melena often indicates digested blood.
Large upper GI bleeds can also produce hematochezia.
NSAIDs, anticoagulants, ulcers, and liver disease increase risk.
priorities: Assess ABCs, perfusion, vital signs, mental status, pain, and amount/appearance of bleeding.
Keep NPO and establish/maintain IV access per orders in acute care.
Report hemodynamic changes immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend blood pressure, heart rate, orthostasis when safe, hemoglobin/hematocrit, stool/emesis, urine output, and mental status.
interventions: Administer ordered IV fluids, proton-pump inhibitor, blood products, and other therapy.
Prepare for endoscopy when indicated.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs can worsen ulcer bleeding.
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase bleeding risk and require clinician-directed holding/reversal decisions.
teaching: Teach avoidance of unapproved NSAIDs, medication adherence, and urgent return for recurrent bleeding or syncope.
delegationScope: Measurement of emesis/stool may be delegated with instructions to save/report findings, but assessment of active bleeding requires licensed-nurse judgment.
examTrap: Assuming black stool is less urgent than bright-red bleeding without checking perfusion.
oneLinePearl: GI bleed severity is measured in perfusion, not color.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology Upper GI Bleeding Guideline

title: Acute Pancreatitis: Pain, Fluids, and Organ Failure
bottomLine: Acute pancreatitis is not just severe abdominal pain; worsening hypovolemia, hypoxemia, renal dysfunction, or systemic inflammatory response can signal severe disease. Supportive care and close trend monitoring are priorities.
recognize: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with nausea/vomiting is classic.
Gallstones and alcohol are common causes; hypertriglyceridemia and medications are other causes.
priorities: Assess pain, hydration/perfusion, respiratory status, abdominal findings, and urine output.
Administer ordered IV fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and early enteral nutrition strategy as tolerated/ordered.
Escalate organ dysfunction promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend vital signs, urine output, oxygenation, BUN/creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, and pain.
interventions: Avoid prolonged routine NPO status when oral/enteral feeding is tolerated and ordered.
Treat the underlying cause such as gallstone obstruction when indicated.
medicationSafety: Opioids may be required for pain but require respiratory/sedation monitoring.
Antibiotics are not routinely used for uncomplicated sterile pancreatitis.
teaching: Teach alcohol avoidance when relevant, gallstone follow-up, medication review, and diet progression per plan.
delegationScope: Routine intake/output and comfort measures may be delegated in stable patients; worsening pain with hemodynamic or respiratory change requires licensed-nurse reassessment.
examTrap: Assuming every patient must remain NPO for days even when early feeding is tolerated and ordered.
oneLinePearl: Pancreatitis becomes dangerous when organs—not just the pancreas—start failing.
sourceBasis: American College of Gastroenterology Acute Pancreatitis Guideline

title: Cirrhosis: Encephalopathy, Bleeding, and Fluid Overload
bottomLine: In decompensated cirrhosis, watch for mental-status change, GI bleeding, infection, renal dysfunction, and worsening ascites. New confusion is not automatically psychiatric—it may be hepatic encephalopathy or another acute trigger.
recognize: Ascites, edema, jaundice, bruising, varices, and encephalopathy reflect decompensation.
Encephalopathy can present as sleep reversal, confusion, asterixis, or decreased consciousness.
Common triggers include infection, GI bleeding, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, and sedatives.
priorities: Assess mental status, bleeding, infection, volume status, respiratory effect of ascites, and bowel pattern.
Report hematemesis, melena, fever, hypotension, or acute confusion urgently.
Administer prescribed lactulose/rifaximin and evaluate response.
assessMonitor: Trend mental status, stool frequency, electrolytes, renal function, weight, abdominal girth when ordered, and signs of bleeding/infection.
interventions: Implement sodium/fluid plan as ordered.
Use fall/aspiration precautions during encephalopathy.
Avoid unnecessary sedatives.
medicationSafety: Lactulose is titrated to clinical response and bowel frequency; excessive diarrhea can cause dehydration/electrolyte loss.
NSAIDs can worsen renal function and bleeding risk in cirrhosis.
teaching: Teach medication adherence, alcohol abstinence when relevant, infection/bleeding warning signs, and avoiding unapproved OTC drugs.
delegationScope: Routine stool count, weight, and intake/output may be delegated with clear parameters; acute mental-status or bleeding assessment requires licensed-nurse evaluation.
examTrap: Holding lactulose because the patient has several soft stools when the prescribed goal has not yet been clarified or encephalopathy is worsening.
oneLinePearl: Cirrhosis plus confusion: search for a trigger and protect the airway.
sourceBasis: AASLD Practice Guidance for Hepatic Encephalopathy and Cirrhosis Complications
